# How to install PHP composer inside a docker container

When setting up a development environment for Laravel using Docker, you often encounter a specific friction point: Composer isn't installed by default in standard PHP images, even when `docker-php-ext-install` and similar commands successfully add extensions like `imagick` or `mcrypt`. If your application relies on `composer dump-autoload` to refresh class maps after running database migrations, the absence of Composer will cause the build process to fail immediately.

A common approach involves appending a command to your `Dockerfile` to install the tool:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -sS https://getcomposer.org/installer | php -- \
    --install-dir=/usr/bin --filename=composer
```

This command downloads the installer script and executes it, placing a binary named `composer` directly into `/usr/bin`. Since `/usr/bin` is part of the standard system `PATH`, this method should theoretically work. However, many developers report encountering the error `exec: "composer": executable file not found in $PATH` when running `docker-compose exec app composer dump-autoload`.

This discrepancy often stems from how Docker Compose constructs the runtime environment or how the specific PHP base image manages its internal `PATH`. While placing the binary in `/usr/bin` is generally correct for Alpine-based images, it can sometimes be inconsistent with Debian-based images (like the `php:7.1.3-fpm` example provided) if the container's default shell environment doesn't explicitly source the system binaries into the active path during execution.

To resolve this, you have two primary strategies depending on your desired level of isolation and portability.

### Explicitly Setting the PATH in the Dockerfile

The most robust solution is to ensure Composer is installed in a location that aligns perfectly with the image's default `PATH` or to explicitly modify the environment variable within the container. If you prefer keeping the binary in `/usr/bin`, you can add a step to refresh the environment or, more commonly, move the installation target to a standard bin directory if one exists, though modifying the `PATH` is the direct fix for existing installations.

You can update your `Dockerfile` to explicitly set the `PATH` after installing Composer:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -sS https://getcomposer.org/installer | php -- \
    --install-dir=/usr/bin --filename=composer && \
    PATH="/usr/bin:${PATH}" && \
    docker-php-ext-install mcrypt pdo_mysql imagick
```

While the `&&` operator chains commands, simply appending to the `PATH` inside the same layer ensures that any subsequent steps or entrypoints inherit this configuration. However, a more persistent fix is often required if the default entrypoint script resets the environment.

### Installing Composer into the User Directory

An alternative approach that frequently circumvents these path resolution issues is installing Composer globally into the application user's home directory. This method avoids reliance on system-level `PATH` configurations which can vary between base images.

You can modify your installation command to target a specific directory, such as `/home/app/.composer`, and then update your shell profile or environment variable:

```dockerfile
RUN curl -sS https://getcomposer.org/installer | php -- \
    --install-dir=/home/app/.composer --filename=composer
ENV PATH="/home/app/.composer:${PATH}"
```

By setting the `PATH` environment variable in the same layer, you guarantee that any process spawned from that imageâincluding your Laravel applicationâwill locate the binary. This approach is particularly useful when dealing with multi-stage builds or when the base image has a restrictive default configuration.

### Verifying the Installation

Once you have rebuilt your image with one of these modifications, verify the installation before running migrations. You can check if the command resolves correctly by inspecting the container:

```bash
docker-compose exec app which composer
```

If this returns a valid path (e.g., `/usr/bin/composer`), the issue is resolved. If it returns nothing, you must revisit your `Dockerfile` to ensure the `PATH` variable was set in a way that persists across the container's lifecycle. Remember that `docker-compose exec` runs commands as the default user defined in your `docker-compose.yml`, so ensuring the binary is accessible to that specific user context is also critical.

For more complex setups involving multiple services or shared volumes, consider checking if your application entrypoint script overrides the shell environment. In some cases, explicitly setting `PATH` in your `docker-compose.yml` under the service definition can be a faster workaround than modifying the base image:

```yaml
environment:
  - PATH=/usr/bin:${PATH}
```

However, embedding this directly into the `Dockerfile` is generally preferred for reproducibility and cache efficiency.
